name: Aher
title: Benjamite mentioned in the genealogy of Chronicles
summary: Aher appears only in 1 Chr 7:12, where he is included in a genealogical context linked to Benjamin and mentioned as the father of Hushim. No further information about his life or work is preserved in the biblical texts. The Hebrew word 'aher' (אַחֵר) means "another," and there is considerable academic debate over whether this is actually a personal name or rather a veiled designation. A prominent hypothesis is that 'Aher' masks a reference to the tribe of Dan, which is notably absent from the genealogies in Chronicles. This interpretation is supported by the fact that Hushim is also identified as a son of Dan in Gen 46:23. The omission of Dan may reflect a deliberate editorial strategy motivated by the tribe's troubled history with idolatry, as described in Judges 18.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Benjamin's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Aher is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as part of a genealogical list related to the tribe of Benjamin. His son Hushim is given as his descendant. This brief note constitutes the only biblical reference to Aher.

keyEvents.title: Possible connection to the tribe of Dan
keyEvents.description: Hushim, who is listed as Aher's son in 1 Chron 7:12, shares a name with Dan's son Hushim as mentioned in Genesis. This similarity in names has given rise to the theory that Aher represents a veiled reference to the tribe of Dan, which is otherwise completely absent from the genealogies in Chronicles.

versions.summary: Aher is a person briefly mentioned in 1 Chronicles in connection with Benjamin's genealogy. He is the father of Hushim. Very little is known about him beyond this genealogical reference, and some biblical scholars identify him with Ahiram or Dan's son Hushim.
versions.title: Benjamite mentioned in the genealogy

versions.summary: Aher appears exclusively in 1 Chr 7:12, where he is mentioned in connection with the genealogy of Benjamin as the father of Hushim. Beyond this brief genealogical note, nothing is known about him. The name 'Aher' is Hebrew for "another," and scholars debate whether it is even a proper name at all. A widespread theory is that 'Aher' serves as a veiled reference to the tribe of Dan—a tribe notably absent from the genealogies in Chronicles. This interpretation is strengthened by the fact that Hushim is also known as a son of Dan in Gen 46:23. The omission of Dan may be linked to the tribe's negative reputation concerning idolatry.
versions.title: Benjamite mentioned in the genealogy of Chronicles
versions.reason: [major] Aher is mentioned in the genealogies of Chronicles and linked to the tribe of Benjamin (or Dan). Although the genealogy extends back to the patriarchal period, the context in which Aher appears – namely the genealogies in 1 Chronicles – relates to the time before or during the united monarchy. However, if Aher actually represents Dan and his son Hushim (cf. Gen 46:23), he belongs to the patriarchal era. Given the uncertainty, 'patriarchs' is defensible, but it should be clarified that this is uncertain.; [minor] The summary is well written, but since this is the third version, it should be further differentiated from earlier versions. footnotes.text: The name 'Aher' (אַחֵר) means 'another' in Hebrew. Several biblical scholars believe this is not a proper name but a paraphrase or euphemism for the tribe of Dan, which is otherwise strikingly absent from the genealogies in 1 Chronicles 2–8. Hushim, who is mentioned as Aher's son, corresponds with Dan's son Hushim in Gen 46:23, which strengthens this theory.

Dan's absence in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles has been the subject of much discussion. One possible explanation is that the chronicler deliberately omitted Dan due to the tribe's association with idolatry (cf. Judg 18), and that 'Aher' ('another') is a deliberate euphemism for Dan's name.

In rabbinic tradition, the connection between Aher and Dan has been discussed. Some rabbinic commentators point out that the tribe of Dan earned a negative reputation because of its association with idols, which may explain the indirect reference in Chronicles.

The context of 1 Chron 7:12 is textually difficult. The verse breaks with the surrounding structure concerning Benjamin's descendants, and several scholars believe it originally belonged to a genealogy of Dan that was either shortened or partially erased during the editing of Chronicles.

The Septuagint version (LXX) of 1 Chron 7:12 differs somewhat from the Hebrew Masoretic text, further highlighting the textual challenges associated with this verse. Variants in ancient manuscripts suggest that the text may have undergone changes during its transmission.
